alt: A vertical timeline of the events in this section, from the 1905 Partition of Bengal and the founding of the Muslim League in 1906 to the Pakistan Resolution of 1940 and the Indian Independence Act of July 1947, with each event coloured by its Key Question.
caption: Forty years of events in one sequence: learn the order before the detail.

alt: Section A is a compulsory source-based question. In Section B candidates answer two of four questions, each split into 4-, 7- and 14-mark parts. The 14-mark answer explains the named factor and at least two others before reaching a reasoned judgement.
caption: The 14-mark essay carries the most marks: three explained factors and a judgement.

after: ## Focus point: why was the Muslim League founded in 1906?
alt: Three causes (Sir Syed’s advice to stay out of Congress, Hindu agitation against the 1905 Partition of Bengal, and the successful Simla Deputation of 1 October 1906) lead to the founding of the League at Dhaka in December 1906, which had three aims.
caption: Bengal was the trigger; protecting Muslim interests as councils grew was the deeper cause.

after: ## Focus point: how did Muslim–Hindu relations change, 1916–27?
alt: A line falls from the Lucknow Pact of 1916, the high point of co-operation, through the Khilafat and Non-Cooperation campaigns, to a breakdown after 1922 marked by communal riots and rival revival movements, ending with the Delhi Proposals of 1927 as a final Muslim offer.
caption: Co-operation peaked in 1916 and broke down after 1922.

after: ## Focus point: why did the Khilafat Movement fail?
alt: The aim of the Khilafat Movement sits above five blows in order: delegations to Britain rejected, the Hijrat of 1920, Gandhi’s suspension of Non-Cooperation after Chauri Chaura in 1922, the Moplah uprising, and Turkey’s abolition of the caliphate in 1924.
caption: Five blows ended the movement; 1922 and 1924 are the two to weigh against each other.

after: ## Focus point: why did Jinnah produce his 14 Points in 1929?
alt: A chain runs from the all-British Simon Commission to the Nehru Report of 1928, the rejection of Jinnah’s amendments and the 14 Points of March 1929. A grid compares the two documents on electorates, the Muslim share of central seats, the balance of power and the protection of Muslim culture.
caption: The 14 Points answered the Nehru Report point by point.

after: ## Focus point: how did the 1945–46 elections change British policy?
alt: A staircase of six steps from the Pakistan Resolution of 1940 through the Cripps Mission, Quit India, the Gandhi–Jinnah talks and the Simla Conference to the League’s victory in the 1945–46 elections. Below, four boxes run from the Cabinet Mission of 1946 to the Indian Independence Act of July 1947.
caption: Every failed solution left the League stronger, until Britain accepted partition.

after: ## Focus point: how important were Jinnah, Iqbal and Rahmat Ali?
alt: Three columns list each leader’s contribution: Jinnah reorganised the League, wrote the 14 Points, led the 1940 Resolution, the 1945–46 elections and the 1946–47 negotiations; Iqbal gave the idea of a Muslim homeland in 1930; Rahmat Ali gave the name “Pakistan” in his 1933 pamphlet but had little political influence.
caption: Two men shaped the idea; one turned it into a state.
